# Exploratory Data Analysis {#sec-eda}


Exploratory data analysis (EDA) examines distributions, relationships, and
irregularities before a final account of findings is written. Its purpose is
to learn what the observed data can show, what they cannot show, and which
questions deserve closer investigation [@nistndexploratory]. This chapter
first states principles that apply across datasets and then develops them
through a case study. The next chapter develops principles for choosing and
evaluating visual displays across the data-science workflow; here, plots
support investigation alongside numerical summaries and checks of the
records.


## EDA Principles


EDA asks what patterns and irregularities are present in a prepared dataset,
and which questions deserve more investigation. Three principles guide the
work:


1. **Explore a question, not a plot collection.** Preparation checks in
   @sec-wrangling establish whether identifiers are unique and joins preserve
   rows. EDA then asks how an outcome is distributed, how groups differ, and
   which observations merit inspection. The same count can serve different
   purposes: missing coordinates may be a preparation diagnostic, while
   differences in missingness by borough may be an EDA question about which
   requests a map leaves out [@yu2024veridical; @tussey2025principles].
2. **Make comparisons fair.** Center, spread, tails, missingness, and group
   size describe different features. A mean alone cannot describe a long
   right tail. Counts from two weekend days and five weekdays have different
   exposure, and copying one area income value onto many requests does not
   create many independent area observations. Choose summaries and plots for
   the comparison, then check that they tell a consistent story
   [@nistndexploratory].
3. **Separate description from inference.** A table can summarize every
   record in the defined scope. A test or interval asks what might happen
   beyond those records and therefore adds assumptions. Those assumptions
   need special care when the groups or thresholds were selected after
   examining the data. A result may also change under a plausible alternative
   time window, treatment of long durations, or geographic grouping. Such
   sensitivity checks show whether a conclusion depends on one analysis
   choice, but cannot repair undercoverage or confounding
   [@yu2024veridical; @wasserstein2016asa].


In practice, EDA cycles through a question, a calculation, an inspection,
and a possible revision. A surprising value may send us back to the source;
a group difference may suggest a better denominator or a more focused
question. The calculation itself does not determine whether a pattern is
important. Interpretation still depends on the eligible records, how the
measurements were made, and what the analysis can support.


## Study Setup


The case study uses the screened requests from @sec-wrangling to revisit the
question in @sec-problem-formulation. The analysis proceeds in this order:


1. Describe the full distribution of recorded closure hours.
2. Compare the three most frequently reported problem-detail groups. The
   frequency rule is set before examining their closure summaries, but it
   does not make the groups random or comparable in other respects.
3. Examine variation by detail, creation date, borough, and matched area to
   see what a citywide median might hide.
4. Use a permutation calculation and bootstrap interval to illustrate how
   inference adds assumptions, then check sensitivity to selected analysis
   choices.


At each step, the four formulation checks in @sec-formulation-checks limit
what the observed differences can establish.


The initial scope report provides an audit of the table that enters this
analysis rather than a second lesson in import and cleaning. The shared
[preparation function](scripts/parking_requests.py) applies the documented
time and problem filters, timestamp parsing, field names, and closure-time
definition from @sec-wrangling. The report then verifies the number of
request identifiers, missing or negative outcomes, and missing coordinates
that affect later spatial comparisons. These checks establish the eligible
set for the present figures; they do not resolve whether reporting behavior
or agency practice differs across groups. The order of analysis is
deliberate: inspect the overall distribution, apply the frequency-based
group rule, examine time and place, and only then consider inferential and
sensitivity calculations. This order makes it possible to distinguish a
comparison specified by the working formulation from an additional pattern
noticed during exploration.


```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from matplotlib_inline.backend_inline import set_matplotlib_formats
from scripts.parking_requests import attach_zcta_context, load_parking_requests

set_matplotlib_formats("svg")

parking = load_parking_requests()

scope_check = pd.Series({
    "requests": len(parking),
    "unique identifiers": parking["request_id"].nunique(),
    "missing closure times": parking["closure_hours"].isna().sum(),
    "negative closure times": parking["closure_hours"].lt(0).sum(),
    "missing coordinates": parking[["latitude", "longitude"]]
        .isna().any(axis=1).sum(),
}, name="count")
scope_check.to_frame()
```


The scope report supports the use of every screened request in the main
closure-time comparison because identifiers are unique and the derived
outcome is present and nonnegative. Missing coordinates do not justify
excluding those requests from a nonspatial distribution, but they do limit
the population represented by a later point map. Treating all missing
fields as a reason for complete-case deletion would conflate these two
eligibility rules. The table also describes a defined week of service
requests rather than a random sample of all parking conditions. A precise
summary of these records can therefore coexist with substantial uncertainty
about unreported incidents or how another week would look. The analysis
will keep the eligible set attached to each result and will interpret
variation in closure time as a mixture of reporting and administrative
processes unless stronger evidence separates them.


## Closure Time by Detail


The overall closure-time distribution establishes which summaries can
represent a typical request and which features require separate attention.
The median divides observed intervals into lower and upper halves, while a
quantile identifies a specified fraction of intervals at or below its
value. The mean reflects every recorded duration and is more sensitive to
the long upper tail. Reporting these quantities together allows readers to
distinguish a typical interval from delayed closures rather than reducing
both to one number. The table below calculates summaries from every
eligible closure interval. The accompanying histogram displays only the
first 24 hours on its horizontal axis to make the dense part of the
distribution legible. That visual limit is not a row exclusion from the
table or subsequent comparisons; the caption and text must make the
difference clear. A later sensitivity calculation explicitly applies a
24-hour row restriction and reports its effect.


```{python}
closure_summary = parking["closure_hours"].agg(
    ["count", "mean", "median", "min", "max"]
).to_frame("value")
for label, probability in [
    ("25th percentile", .25), ("75th percentile", .75),
    ("90th percentile", .90), ("99th percentile", .99),
]:
    closure_summary.loc[label] = parking["closure_hours"].quantile(probability)
closure_summary = closure_summary.rename(index={
    "count": "requests",
    "mean": "mean (hours)",
    "median": "median (hours)",
    "min": "minimum (hours)",
    "max": "maximum (hours)",
    "25th percentile": "25th percentile (hours)",
    "75th percentile": "75th percentile (hours)",
    "90th percentile": "90th percentile (hours)",
    "99th percentile": "99th percentile (hours)",
})
closure_summary.round(2)
```


```{python}
#| label: fig-eda-closure
#| fig-cap: "Recorded closure times for eligible illegal-parking requests. The display stops at 24 hours; the numerical summary includes longer intervals."
#| fig-format: svg
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.8))
ax.hist(parking["closure_hours"], bins=np.arange(0, 24.5, .5),
        color="#4477aa", edgecolor="white")
ax.set(xlabel="Recorded closure time (hours)", ylabel="Requests",
       xlim=(0, 24))
plt.show()
```


The median closure interval is about 1.67 hours, while the mean is about 3.51
hours. The 90th percentile is about 8.73 hours, the 99th percentile is about
23.58 hours, and the maximum is nearly 200 hours. Read these summaries
together:


- The **median** describes the middle request: half of recorded intervals
  are shorter and half longer.
- The **mean** is larger because it is pulled upward by the long right tail.
- The **upper percentiles and maximum** show that a small share of requests
  took much longer than the typical request.


Thus, “requests close in about two hours” is incomplete. A large interval
could be valid, a timestamp correction, or an operational exception; its
size alone does not show which. The group comparison therefore reports
medians and quartiles alongside means.


The group rule uses request frequency, not closure time, to choose categories.
The code calculates each selected group's count, center, spread, and upper
quantile while retaining the provider's original category labels. Similar
labels are not combined without evidence that they share an operational
meaning. A different week could produce a different list of frequent
categories.


The empirical cumulative distribution provides a second way to compare the
groups. At a closure time $t$, its vertical value is the fraction of requests
closed by time $t$. For example, a value of 0.70 at $t=2$ hours means that
70% of the group's recorded requests closed within two hours. The curves
allow comparisons at any threshold without assuming that the distributions
have the same shape. Since both the group rule and analysis were developed
using this week, later inferential calculations remain exploratory.


```{python}
top_details = parking["problem_detail"].value_counts().head(3).index.tolist()
top = parking.loc[parking["problem_detail"].isin(top_details)].copy()
detail_summary = top.groupby("problem_detail")["closure_hours"].agg(
    requests="count",
    mean_hours="mean",
    median_hours="median",
    lower_quartile=lambda values: values.quantile(.25),
    upper_quartile=lambda values: values.quantile(.75),
    ninetieth_percentile=lambda values: values.quantile(.90),
).reindex(top_details)
detail_summary.round(2)
```


```{python}
#| label: fig-eda-detail-ecdf
#| fig-cap: "Empirical cumulative distributions of closure time for the three most reported details. The horizontal axis stops at 24 hours."
#| fig-format: svg
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.8))
for detail in top_details:
    durations = np.sort(top.loc[
        top["problem_detail"].eq(detail), "closure_hours"
    ].to_numpy())
    fractions = np.arange(1, len(durations) + 1) / len(durations)
    ax.step(durations, fractions, where="post", label=detail)
ax.set(xlabel="Recorded closure time (hours)",
       ylabel="Proportion closed by this time", xlim=(0, 24), ylim=(0, 1))
ax.legend()
plt.show()
```


Blocked Hydrant has the largest median of the three groups, about 2.05 hours,
followed by Posted Parking Sign Violation at 1.62 hours and Blocked Sidewalk
at 1.18 hours. The hydrant group's median exceeds the sidewalk group's by
about 0.86 hours, or 52 minutes. Their distributions overlap substantially,
so the difference in medians does not mean that every hydrant request took
longer than every sidewalk request. The cumulative curves show the
proportion closed by any time on the horizontal axis; they retain more
distributional information than a comparison of three means. Neither the
table nor the plot identifies why the groups differ.


## Variation Across Groups


Temporal and geographic stratification examines whether a pooled group
contrast combines different request mixes. Creation date identifies when
a report entered the service system, whereas closure time is the subsequent
elapsed interval; grouping by creation date does not assign a request to
the date on which it closed. The first table reports the daily volume of
eligible requests, so each row has a one-day observation period. The
second table counts the three selected problem details by borough and
shows whether their relative frequencies differ across places. These
tables are descriptive checks on composition, not estimates of the
frequency of illegal parking on the street. A difference in group mix can
help explain why a citywide closure-time summary differs from a
within-borough summary, but the tables alone do not establish the agency
process that generated either pattern.


```{python}
daily_counts = parking.groupby(parking["created_at"].dt.date).size()
daily_counts.to_frame("requests")
```


```{python}
borough_counts = pd.crosstab(top["borough"], top["problem_detail"])
borough_counts.loc[:, top_details]
```


Recorded daily volume ranges from 1,563 on September 6 to 2,080 on September
10. The counts alone do not establish a weekday effect because they cover
only one occurrence of each day of the week. The borough table shows that
the mix of problem details also varies by place: Manhattan has more Posted
Parking Sign Violation requests than Blocked Hydrant requests, whereas
Brooklyn has the opposite ordering. Geographic composition can therefore
affect the citywide comparison. A borough label still represents a broad
area and cannot identify the practices of an individual precinct.


Area context raises a different exploratory question and changes the unit
at which a comparison is valid. The area-context workflow in
@sec-zcta-context-merge explains the five-digit ZIP-label match to 2024
American Community Survey (ACS) estimates for ZIP Code Tabulation Areas
(ZCTAs), including its geographic limitations [@census2023zip]. This chapter
reuses the checked lookup through `attach_zcta_context()` instead of
repeating the preparation code.
The resulting table still has one row per request, so an income estimate
appears on every request whose ZIP label matches the same ZCTA. Those
copies do not constitute independent observations of area income. The
comparison below first aggregates closure time to one row per matched
ZCTA, records the number of requests supporting each area median, and then
groups areas by estimated income. Its target is variation among area
summaries, not the relationship between a reporter's income and that
reporter's closure time.


```{python}
with_context = attach_zcta_context(parking)
with_context["_merge"].value_counts()
```


```{python}
areas = with_context.loc[with_context["_merge"].eq("both")].groupby(
    "zcta", as_index=False
).agg(
    requests=("request_id", "size"),
    median_closure_hours=("closure_hours", "median"),
    median_household_income=("median_household_income", "first"),
)
eligible_areas = areas.loc[
    areas["requests"].ge(20) & areas["median_household_income"].notna()
].copy()
eligible_areas["income_quartile"] = pd.qcut(
    eligible_areas["median_household_income"], 4,
    labels=["lowest", "lower-middle", "upper-middle", "highest"],
)
area_summary = eligible_areas.groupby(
    "income_quartile", observed=True
).agg(
    areas=("zcta", "size"),
    requests=("requests", "sum"),
    median_of_area_medians=("median_closure_hours", "median"),
)
area_summary.round(2)
```


The join matches 13,033 of 13,040 requests. Among areas with at least 20
requests and a reported median household income, 149 ZCTAs enter the grouped
comparison. Their median closure times differ across income quartiles, but
the ordering is not monotone: the lower-middle quartile has a higher median
of area medians than the lowest or upper-middle quartile. The minimum count
of 20 is a transparent stability rule, not a guarantee of accurate area
estimates. The ACS income values describe an earlier period and have
sampling uncertainty; the request-to-ZCTA match also has geographic limits
[@census2026american]. This table supports a question about area-level
association, not a conclusion about residents' incomes or an income effect
on individual requests.


Subgroup composition can also change the direction of an overall
comparison. Simpson's paradox describes cases where an association in
aggregated data weakens or reverses after data are divided into subgroups
defined by a third variable
[@simpson1951interpretation]. The following hypothetical example
illustrates the arithmetic with treatment success rates. Treatment A has a
higher success rate than treatment B in both risk groups, but A is used much
more often for high-risk cases. The pooled rates therefore favor B. The
values are constructed for instruction and do not describe a medical study.


```{python}
simpson = pd.DataFrame({
    "risk": ["Lower", "Lower", "Higher", "Higher"],
    "treatment": ["A", "B", "A", "B"],
    "successes": [81, 234, 192, 55],
    "cases": [87, 270, 263, 80],
})
simpson["success_rate"] = simpson["successes"] / simpson["cases"]
within_risk = simpson.pivot(
    index="risk", columns="treatment", values="success_rate"
)
case_shares = simpson.pivot(
    index="risk", columns="treatment", values="cases"
)
case_shares = case_shares.div(case_shares.sum(axis=0), axis=1)
pooled = simpson.groupby("treatment")["successes"].sum() / simpson.groupby(
    "treatment"
)["cases"].sum()
result = pd.concat([within_risk, pooled.rename("Pooled").to_frame().T])
result["A case share"] = case_shares["A"]
result["B case share"] = case_shares["B"]
result.loc["Pooled", ["A case share", "B case share"]] = 1
result.round(3)
```


The table makes the changing weights visible: treatment A has a larger share
of its cases in the higher-risk group, where success is less common for both
treatments. The pooled row summarizes success rates, while the case-share
columns show each treatment's composition.


This reversal does not show which treatment is more effective. Risk group
may be related to treatment assignment, and other differences may remain
within each stratum. Analysts should report the overall and within-group
summaries and explain why the stratifying variable matters before drawing a
causal conclusion. The later visualization chapter develops small-multiple
displays that make subgroup comparisons easier to inspect
[@armstrong2014visualizing]. It applies this approach with `facet_grid()`
(see @sec-visualization).


## Uncertainty Assessment


A hypothesis test can be part of EDA when its assumptions and limited
purpose are explicit. Consider the median closure-time difference between
Blocked Hydrant and Blocked Sidewalk requests. For the observed week, that
difference is descriptive and needs no test. A test addresses a different
question: under a model in which requests from the two detail groups have
exchangeable closure-time distributions, how unusual would the observed
difference be? The permutation calculation below pools the two groups and
reallocates their labels while preserving their sizes. Its two-sided
statistic is the absolute difference between medians. A bootstrap interval
separately resamples requests within each group to show variability under
an independent-request model.


The appropriate test depends on the outcome scale, comparison structure,
and sampling or assignment process. The table links common questions to
Python functions and states the null or design condition each function
addresses [@scipy2026statistical; @statsmodels2026proportion;
@statsmodels2026contingency]. This guide is not
an automatic decision rule: inspect the data and define the target contrast
before choosing a test [@nistndexploratory].


| Question and design | Test and Python function | Null or key condition |
|---|---|---|
| Is one numerical mean equal to a reference value? | One-sample $t$ test, `scipy.stats.ttest_1samp` | Population mean equals the reference value. |
| Do two independent groups have different means? | Welch $t$ test, `scipy.stats.ttest_ind(..., equal_var=False)` | Population means are equal; equal variances are not assumed. |
| Do paired measurements have different means? | Paired $t$ test, `scipy.stats.ttest_rel` | Mean within-pair difference is zero; pairs are independent. |
| Do three or more independent groups have equal means? | One-way ANOVA, `scipy.stats.f_oneway`; use `equal_var=False` for Welch ANOVA | All group means are equal; classical ANOVA assumes equal variances, and follow-up comparisons need multiplicity control. |
| Are two categorical variables associated? | Chi-square test, `scipy.stats.chi2_contingency` | Variables are independent; the large-sample approximation must be adequate. |
| Is a sparse $2\times2$ table associated? | Fisher exact test, `scipy.stats.fisher_exact` | Tests association conditional on fixed table margins. |
| Does one proportion equal a benchmark, or do two proportions differ? | Binomial test, `scipy.stats.binomtest`; two-proportion test, `statsmodels.stats.proportion.proportions_ztest` | Proportions equal the stated benchmark or each other; samples must follow the test's independent-sampling design. |
| Do paired binary outcomes change? | McNemar's test, `statsmodels.stats.contingency_tables.mcnemar` | The two paired marginal proportions are equal; pairs are independent. |
| Are two numerical variables associated? | Pearson, `scipy.stats.pearsonr`; Spearman, `scipy.stats.spearmanr` | Tests zero linear correlation or zero rank correlation, respectively. |
| Do independent groups differ in rank distributions? | Mann--Whitney, `scipy.stats.mannwhitneyu`; Kruskal--Wallis, `scipy.stats.kruskal` | Tests equal distributions or rank locations under their assumptions; neither automatically tests equal medians. |
| Is a chosen statistic unusual under exchangeable labels? | Permutation test, `scipy.stats.permutation_test` | Labels can be reassigned under the null; the statistic must match the question. |


The first code example uses the contingency table from the three most
frequent details to ask whether the observed detail mix varies by borough.
The chi-square test evaluates independence, while Cramér's $V$ summarizes
the strength of the association. The expected cell counts help assess
whether the chi-square approximation is adequate. Because the details were
selected by frequency in this same week, this is an exploratory calculation,
not a confirmatory test of a prespecified hypothesis.


```{python}
from scipy.stats import chi2_contingency

detail_by_borough = pd.crosstab(top["problem_detail"], top["borough"])
chi_square = chi2_contingency(detail_by_borough)
sample_size = detail_by_borough.to_numpy().sum()
cramers_v = np.sqrt(
    chi_square.statistic
    / (sample_size * min(detail_by_borough.shape[0] - 1,
                         detail_by_borough.shape[1] - 1))
)
display(detail_by_borough)
pd.Series({
    "chi-square statistic": chi_square.statistic,
    "degrees of freedom": chi_square.dof,
    "p-value": chi_square.pvalue,
    "smallest expected cell count": chi_square.expected_freq.min(),
    "Cramer's V": cramers_v,
}).to_frame("value")
```


The next example uses Welch's test to compare arithmetic mean closure hours
for hydrant and sidewalk requests. It answers a different question from the
median comparison below, and the long right tail can make the mean sensitive
to a small number of long intervals. The request-level calculation also
assumes independent observations, although requests may share locations,
times, or administrative conditions.


```{python}
from scipy.stats import ttest_ind

hydrant = top.loc[
    top["problem_detail"].eq("Blocked Hydrant"), "closure_hours"
].dropna().to_numpy()
sidewalk = top.loc[
    top["problem_detail"].eq("Blocked Sidewalk"), "closure_hours"
].dropna().to_numpy()
welch_test = ttest_ind(hydrant, sidewalk, equal_var=False)
pd.Series({
    "hydrant mean (hours)": hydrant.mean(),
    "sidewalk mean (hours)": sidewalk.mean(),
    "mean difference (hours)": hydrant.mean() - sidewalk.mean(),
    "Welch t statistic": welch_test.statistic,
    "Welch degrees of freedom": welch_test.df,
    "two-sided p-value": welch_test.pvalue,
}).to_frame("value")
```


Requests from one week may share time, location, or agency conditions,
which weakens a simple independence model. A statistical test does not
correct those design limitations, and selecting a test after searching
many groupings can make its nominal $p$-value misleading
[@wasserstein2016asa]. Rank-based tests such as Mann--Whitney and
Kruskal--Wallis do not automatically test a difference in medians. Likewise,
a bootstrap interval estimates uncertainty under a resampling scheme; it
is not itself a hypothesis test. When many outcomes, subgroups, or
alternatives are examined, report that search and do not treat a threshold
such as 0.05 as a mechanical decision rule [@wasserstein2016asa].


```{python}
hydrant = top.loc[
    top["problem_detail"].eq("Blocked Hydrant"), "closure_hours"
].dropna().to_numpy()
sidewalk = top.loc[
    top["problem_detail"].eq("Blocked Sidewalk"), "closure_hours"
].dropna().to_numpy()
observed_gap = np.median(hydrant) - np.median(sidewalk)

rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
bootstrap_gaps = np.array([
    np.median(rng.choice(hydrant, size=len(hydrant), replace=True))
    - np.median(rng.choice(sidewalk, size=len(sidewalk), replace=True))
    for _ in range(2000)
])
interval = np.quantile(bootstrap_gaps, [.025, .975])
combined = np.concatenate([hydrant, sidewalk])
permuted_gaps = np.array([
    np.median(shuffled[:len(hydrant)])
    - np.median(shuffled[len(hydrant):])
    for shuffled in (rng.permutation(combined) for _ in range(2000))
])
extreme = np.count_nonzero(np.abs(permuted_gaps) >= abs(observed_gap))
p_value = (extreme + 1) / (len(permuted_gaps) + 1)
pd.Series({
    "observed median gap (hours)": observed_gap,
    "bootstrap lower endpoint (hours)": interval[0],
    "bootstrap upper endpoint (hours)": interval[1],
    "permutation p-value": p_value,
}).to_frame("value").round(4)
```


The observed median gap is about 0.865 hours, and the bootstrap interval is
approximately 0.712 to 1.016 hours. The estimated permutation $p$-value is
about 0.0005, with the added one in the numerator and denominator preventing
a reported zero from a finite set of permutations. These results show that
the observed separation is large relative to these relabelings and
resamples. They do not establish that the detail label causes a closure-time
difference. Requests may be related through place, time, repeat reporting,
or agency practice, and the analysis was chosen after inspection of this
week. The bootstrap interval does not include uncertainty from coverage,
measurement, or group selection. A $p$-value should not be read as the
probability that the null hypothesis is true or as a measure of practical
importance [@wasserstein2016asa].


Sensitivity analysis quantifies how much a descriptive result changes
under defensible alternatives to the primary calculation. Yu and Barter
emphasize that choices made during cleaning, preprocessing, and analysis
can affect a reported finding [@yu2024veridical]. The first check below
restricts closure intervals to at most 24 hours to assess the influence
of the long upper tail; it does not classify longer intervals as invalid.
The remaining checks calculate the same hydrant-minus-sidewalk median gap
within each borough, holding the outcome definition and group labels fixed
while changing geographic composition. These are targeted perturbations
of the eligible set rather than an exhaustive search for a desired result.
The table reports group sizes alongside gaps because a large contrast
based on few requests deserves a different interpretation from a similar
contrast based on many. Neither sensitivity check removes confounding or
extends the conclusion beyond the observed week.


```{python}
def median_gap(frame):
    left = frame.loc[
        frame["problem_detail"].eq("Blocked Hydrant"), "closure_hours"
    ]
    right = frame.loc[
        frame["problem_detail"].eq("Blocked Sidewalk"), "closure_hours"
    ]
    return pd.Series({
        "hydrant_requests": len(left),
        "sidewalk_requests": len(right),
        "median_gap_hours": left.median() - right.median(),
    })

sensitivity = pd.DataFrame({
    "all requests": median_gap(top),
    "closure at most 24 hours": median_gap(
        top.loc[top["closure_hours"].le(24)]
    ),
}).T
for borough in sorted(top["borough"].dropna().unique()):
    sensitivity.loc[borough.title()] = median_gap(
        top.loc[top["borough"].eq(borough)]
    )
sensitivity[["hydrant_requests", "sidewalk_requests"]] = sensitivity[[
    "hydrant_requests", "sidewalk_requests"
]].astype(int)
sensitivity.round(3)
```


The all-request median gap is about 0.865 hours and changes little, to about
0.848 hours, after intervals above 24 hours are excluded. The geographic
comparisons are less uniform: the gap is about 1.07 hours in Brooklyn and
1.09 hours in Queens, but only 0.10 hours in the Bronx and approximately
zero in Manhattan. Staten Island has a larger gap, but its comparison uses
only 54 hydrant and 34 sidewalk requests. Group sizes and possible
differences in case mix or processing limit the interpretation of these
contrasts. The pooled result therefore does not describe every borough
equally well.


Exploration has answered the initial descriptive question for the recorded
week: closure-time distributions differ among the three most reported
details, with a long right tail and the largest median among Blocked Hydrant
requests. It has also identified conditions for a more focused next
analysis. A future question could compare those details within borough and
creation-time strata across multiple weeks, while documenting changes in
request volume and closure practices. A causal question about why closure
times differ would require a design that addresses confounding and the
meaning of the recorded outcome. The ZCTA analysis similarly motivates
area-level questions but does not turn area income into a request-level
explanation. EDA makes observed patterns and the limits of their
interpretation explicit enough to guide that next question.

These exercises use the distributed request archive and, where indicated,
`data/zcta_context.csv`. Report the record counts behind each summary,
state units and exclusions, and distinguish descriptive findings from
claims about processes outside the observed week.

::: {#exr-eda-time}
Examine whether long-closure requests vary by the hour when a request was
created. Define a request as long-closure when its closure time is at least
two hours; exclude requests without a usable closure time and report their
number.

a. Divide creation hours into four six-hour intervals and state their
   boundaries. Construct a contingency table of interval by long-closure
   status, showing both counts and within-interval proportions. Include the
   eligible request count for each interval.
b. Repeat the table for the three most frequent problem details. Identify one
   contrast that changes across intervals and compare its group sizes.
c. Compare the binary outcome with the continuous closure-time summaries.
   Explain why either table alone cannot distinguish a time-of-day pattern
   from changes in location, reporting behavior, or case mix.
:::

::: {#exr-eda-area}
Revisit the ZCTA comparison under alternative inclusion rules.

a. Construct one row per matched ZCTA with request count, median closure time,
   and ACS median household income. Report missing income values and explain
   why the area, rather than the request, is the observational unit here.
b. Compare the quartile summary using minimum request counts of 10, 20, and
   40 per ZCTA. State how many areas and requests enter each version.
c. Assess whether the direction of the area-level association is stable.
   Describe at least two limitations of a postal ZIP to ZCTA string match.
:::

::: {#exr-eda-inference}
Evaluate a proposed claim that hydrant requests generally take longer to
close than sidewalk requests.

a. Reproduce the observed median difference, bootstrap interval, and
   permutation calculation using a documented random seed.
b. Repeat the median comparison within each borough with at least 50
   requests of each detail. Report the eligible group counts.
c. Write a conclusion that separates the observed week's pattern, inference
   under the resampling assumptions, and the unsupported causal claim.
:::
